transcript:
MEETING HEADER:
Date: 2026-07-20 10:00 PDT
Duration: ~45 minutes
Attendees: Lena M., Samir P., Ava C. (Redwood) — Priya N., Marcus L., Elena T. (Novus)

00:00 Lena: Okay everyone, thanks for hopping on. Quick agenda: recap last week's pilot numbers, sizing adjustments, autoscaling policy and burst planning, and then next steps. Priya you said Marcus would share traces — is that still on track?
00:18 Marcus: Yeah sorry for the delay, we cleaned the traces, should be uploaded by end of day Friday, but I can try to get an earlier slice. It's basically production-ish traffic from the pre-prod environment.
00:30 Samir: Perfect. I used the rough histogram you sent last week to run the estimator — quick note, transcription, I mean the estimator shows a higher p95 than expected because of a long tail in user requests, lots of 6–8k token contexts that blow the kv cache sizes.
00:45 Priya: Right, we've had a handful of long sessions, especially with longer chart history being pasted in. We're trying to balance that with latency SLAs.
01:00 Ava: Quick clarifying point — when you say p95, is that for end-to-end response time including network or purely inference?
01:06 Elena: In our charts it's application-side, so it includes some routing, but we've also got raw model inference times in the traces.
01:15 Samir: Okay good. So the numbers I have from last week's hosted run: baseline peak qps ~18, average tokens per request ~720, and observed p95 inference time ~450ms on the hosted endpoint for the model we're testing. That's higher than the team's target of p95 <350ms.
01:34 Lena: The goal for this pilot was predictable latency under Dedicated and to validate autoscaling so you don't hit those 450ms spikes.
01:42 Marcus: On capacity we need to think about bursts from report generation jobs — those are short but very spiky. They can triple qps for 30–90 seconds.
01:52 Samir: Right — for spiky workloads we recommend a two-tier policy: a steady-state pool (min nodes) sized for typical sustained qps, plus a burst pool reserved for pre-warmed GPUs that can instantaneously handle a multiple of steady qps.
02:05 Priya: Can you spell out exact numbers? We've heard "min/max" and "burst" but need concrete starting points.
02:12 Samir: Based on the histogram I modelled three profiles: conservative, expected, and peak. For your expected profile (median workload), a dedicated pool of 2 A100-equivalent GPUs with continuous autoscale to 6 handles steady spikes. For peak (the report jobs) we'd recommend allowing a burst up to 4 additional GPUs — so min 2, target max 12 (6 steady + 4 burst headroom + buffer), but the exact max depends on your cost comfort.
02:41 Elena: So min 2, max 12, burst 4 — got it. How do warm pools work?
02:49 Ava: Warm pool GPUs are kept with the runtime and model loaded so they can accept traffic instantly. They cost less than fully provisioned reserved instances in some contract models but you pay for the warm memory. The important bits are cooldown windows and pre-warm thresholds. For your use case we recommend a warm-pool of 2 GPUs with a 30–60s warmup, and a cooldown of 2–5 minutes so they don't spin down immediately after a short spike.
03:12 Marcus: That helps. Do we do scaling by QPS or by token throughput?
03:18 Samir: Good question — we prefer a combined signal: primary metric QPS with a secondary metric of tokens/sec or GPU utilization. For long-tail token requests it's safer to trigger on tokens/sec because a few long requests can saturate memory and slow down many short ones. So policy: scale up if QPS > threshold for 30s OR tokens/sec > threshold, and scale down after 3–5 minutes of underutilization.
03:42 Priya: How about model fallbacks — if the dedicated pool is at capacity, can we route to a smaller quantized variant?
03:49 Samir: Yes — smart routing can fall back to a quantized variant or a lower-memory model to keep latency bounded. We usually set a policy to failover only when p95 cross a critical threshold and with a knob to control quality degradation. We'll propose two tiers: primary high-accuracy model, fallback quantized model with slightly lower quality but faster latency.
04:07 Elena: Any concerns about KV cache eviction with the warm pool? We saw cache misses last week.
04:13 Ava: The KV cache is per-GPU session; warm GPUs will have model and sometimes prefix caching, but if the session is different you'll still miss. We recommend application-level prefix caching for the common prompts (auth flows, common instructions) so warm pools are more effective. Also ensure session affinity when possible so you keep the KV cache hot for conversational users.
04:35 Lena: On costs — this sizing (min2/max12, 4-burst) increases committed capacity. Priya, are you okay with a visible headroom for the pilot?
04:43 Priya: We can accept it for the pilot if we can get better cost estimates. Marcus, procurement will want clear upper bounds.
04:50 Marcus: Yes finance will want a worst-case monthly run rate.
04:54 Samir: I'll include an estimated monthly burn for min/avg/peak in the spreadsheet — I model token costs, GPU-hour cost, and an amortized warm-pool surcharge.
05:03 Priya: On SLAs, we want p95 for interactive flows <350ms. For batch/report jobs we're OK with a higher tail. Can you guarantee routing behavior so interactive flows are prioritized?
05:16 Ava: Yes, Redwood route policies can tag interactive routes and use lower-batch, lower-latency queues; autoscaler respects route priorities. We'll propose a canary policy that keeps 1–2 GPUs pinned for interactive routes in addition to warm pool.
05:28 Elena: For benchmarking, what data do you need from us?
05:31 Samir: Prometheus traces with QPS, tokens per request histogram, and sample request/response pairs. If you can, please mark which flows are interactive vs batch. Also environment details (sequence lengths typical) and any custom tokenization.
05:45 Marcus: We'll drop a link in the shared drive today.
05:48 Lena: Great. Any blockers on the security/compliance side for bringing dedicated into a VPC?
05:53 Priya: We're okay with VPC, just need KMS integration and audit logs — we reviewed Redwood's SOC2 doc last week and it looked fine.
06:01 Ava: Confirmed — we have KMS/HSM integrations and audit logging; I'll attach the security artifact in the follow-up.
06:07 Samir: Next, quick note on autoscaler cooldowns: avoid aggressive downscaling. With heavy memory workloads, scale down too fast can evict caches and increase latency. We recommend a 3–5 minute cooldown and a conservative downscale step size (remove 1 GPU at a time).
06:23 Priya: Sounds reasonable.
06:26 Lena: Okay to summarize — Samir/Ava update sizing and autoscaling doc with warm-pool and cooldown recommendations; Marcus/Elena to upload traces and label interactive flows; Lena to send pricing and contract; schedule on-site benchmark week of 7/27 pending trace review.
06:41 Priya: That's good. One last thing — any known limitations with quantized fallbacks for our model footprint?
06:48 Samir: The fallback quality delta depends on quantization recipe; we'll include recommended quantization profiles and expected latency delta in the doc. For your current model, expect ~20–30% faster p95 with 8-bit quantization but some edge-case hallucination risk — we'll run evals against your prompt set.
07:06 Marcus: Fine. We'll review.
07:09 Lena: Thanks everyone — we'll send notes and artifacts. Meeting adjourned.

TRANSCRIPT NOTES: occasional transcription artifacts (K V cache, kevy cache) and speaker overlaps. End of export.
